title: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} Keyfob — 125 kHz Rewritable Access Fob
summary: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} keyfobs contain a rewritable 125 kHz LF RFID chip (ISO/IEC 18000-2 air-interface, 512-bit EEPROM, 100,000 write-cycle endurance, 32-bit password lock) that can be programmed and reprogrammed with new ID data. Unlike the read-only {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} / EM4200, {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} supports {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, HID Prox H10301, Indala and AWID emulation from a single chip — the specification anchor for tenant-turnover reuse, multi-protocol integrator inventory, SIA OSDP v2.2 retrofit of Wiegand-26 legacy readers, and the LF leg of any LF → HF AES-128 migration.
heroPoints: Rewritable 512-bit EEPROM with 100,000 write-cycle endurance and optional 32-bit password lock ({chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:name} datasheet) — reuse a fob across many tenant cycles without replacing hardware.

Multi-protocol emulation: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} is configurable to emulate {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, HID Prox H10301 26-bit, Indala and AWID — a single SKU replaces a library of format-specific fobs held by integrators for on-site commissioning.

LF security posture is stated explicitly: the 125 kHz air interface has no cryptography — {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} is correct for tenant-reuse, OSDP retrofit and legacy-reader envelopes, NOT for enterprise access where AES-128 HF (DESFire EV3 / Plus SE / iCLASS SE) is the required control.

sections.title: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} vs {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} vs {chip:atmel-t5577:name} — which LF chip to specify
sections.intro: All three are 125 kHz LF chips sharing ISO/IEC 18000-2 physical-layer behaviour, but their memory, emulation breadth and ops profiles differ. The choice is usually driven by tenant-turnover cadence and how many legacy protocols the integrator's inventory has to cover.

before: 64-bit factory-written ID — one chip, one identity, permanently
Read-only — cannot be reprogrammed; each tenant turnover mandates a new fob
Emulates only native {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} — no HID Prox, no Indala, no AWID
Lowest unit cost but highest lifetime cost in high-turnover environments (40-60 % higher once reissue is counted)
No password cell, no write-lock — no protection because there is nothing writable to protect
Best fit: single-issuance, low-turnover, LF-only legacy reader where the fob is expected to be disposable
after: 512-bit EEPROM, field-rewritable by any 125 kHz writer that knows the 32-bit password
100,000 write-cycle rating — outlasts the ABS housing by 2-3 orders of magnitude
Emulates {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, HID Prox H10301 26-bit, Indala, AWID, ISO 11784/11785 FDX-B
Optional 32-bit password prevents casual overwrites; write-lock bit seals the config permanently after personalisation
Integrator inventory collapses from 4-6 chip SKUs to one — programmed on-site to match the client's reader
Best fit: multi-tenant residential, storage, co-working, OSDP retrofit, integrator test inventory

sections.title: Quantified cost case for rewritable over read-only in high-turnover sites
sections.intro: Read-only fobs win the invoice and lose the ledger. Over a high-turnover lease the cheaper sticker price quietly becomes the more expensive programme — here is where the money actually goes, and why the rewritable chip is the one procurement signs off on. The baseline it beats is the read-only [EM4100 card](/products/rfid-cards/em4100-rfid-card/).

sections.title: Deployment roadmap — LF {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} within a multi-year reader fleet
sections.intro: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} sits inside a life-cycle that typically begins with a legacy HID Prox / Wiegand-26 panel already in the building, ends with an HF AES-128 reader, and runs through a 12-24 month dual-technology bridge. Proud Tek staging follows the pattern below.

items.label: Year 0 · Incumbent LF-only panel — Wiegand-26 / HID Prox
items.text: Site has HID ProxPoint / AWID / Indala readers already installed. {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} is programmed to emulate the existing HID Prox H10301 format with the correct facility code and card-number range; issuance is drop-in compatible with zero panel change.

items.label: Year 0-1 · OSDP v2.2 retrofit of the 5-wire Wiegand interface
items.text: Reader-to-panel wiring is upgraded from Wiegand 5-wire to SIA OSDP v2.2 (RS-485, Secure Channel Protocol). The keyfob chemistry does not change — {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} still presents the HID Prox number — but the reader-to-panel link gets authenticated and encrypted. This closes the easiest credential-line attack without touching the fob fleet.

items.label: Year 1-2 · Dual-technology issuance — LF {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} + HF DESFire EV3
items.text: New hires / tenants receive dual-frequency fobs carrying both an {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} LF chip and a DESFire EV3 HF chip. Old LF-only readers continue to accept the fob on 125 kHz while new HF readers start rolling out for high-security zones (main entrance, server rooms, cash office).

items.label: Year 2-3 · HF rollout completion and LF retirement
items.text: HF readers cover 100 % of controlled openings. The LF half of the dual-frequency fob is no longer authoritative — only the DESFire EV3 authentication grants access. EM4305-only fobs are phased out for primary access and retained for low-risk carriers: guest parking, tenant-reuse amenities, storage lockers.

items.label: Year 3+ · Operational steady state with documented residual risk
items.text: Reference clients across multi-tenant-residential, storage-facility, co-working, SIA-OSDP retrofit, HID-Prox-emulation, integrator test-inventory and LF-to-HF migration EM4305-keyfob programmes operate on per-vertical cadences for audit, hardware refresh, key rotation and supplier review. the LF residual (tenant amenities, storage unit access) is explicitly scoped in the site's access-control policy as a low-value envelope where Proxmark / Flipper clone risk is accepted, and the HF AES-128 envelope carries the high-value openings.

sections.title: One EM4305, every legacy format your readers already speak
sections.intro: The reason integrators standardise on EM4305 is boring and decisive: one rewritable chip impersonates the whole 125 kHz zoo. Program it on a bench writer and the same fob answers to an EM4100 panel, an HID Prox reader, an Indala head or an AWID head — no per-format SKU, no guessing which legacy system the building runs. It is still LF, so walk the [125 kHz vs 13.56 MHz](/compare/125khz-vs-13.56mhz-rfid/) line before you bet a high-security door on it.

image.alt: Diagram of a central EM4305 chip fanning out to five legacy 125 kHz formats it can emulate: EM4100 / EM4200 native 64 or 128-bit ID, HID Prox H10301 26-bit, Indala 26 or 27-bit, AWID, and ISO 11784 / 11785 FDX-B, with a note that LF has no cryptography and the ID is clone-readable.

bullets: Native EM4100 / EM4200: the 64-bit or 128-bit read-only ID every legacy LF panel already accepts.
HID Prox H10301: program the 26-bit facility code and card number and the fob answers HID ProxPoint readers directly.
Indala and AWID: the other two legacy Wiegand dialects, covered from the same chip.
ISO 11784 / 11785 FDX-B: the animal-ID heritage that also gives the silicon its wide -25 to +85 °C temperature spec.

sections.title: Anatomy of the fob — coil, chip, and the shell that survives a keyring
sections.intro: Electrically a 125 kHz fob is almost nothing: a many-turn copper coil, the EM4305 die, and potting. The engineering decision that actually reaches the buyer is the housing — ABS for cheap-and-colourful, platinum-cured silicone for IP68 wash-down, epoxy for a seamless outdoor drop — all finished on a 304 / 316 stainless split ring. Want the same chip in a card instead of a fob? The [EM4100 RFID card](/products/rfid-cards/em4100-rfid-card/) shares the silicon.

image.alt: Cutaway of a 125 kHz LF keyfob labelling five parts: the housing (ABS, silicone rated IP68, or epoxy), a many-turn copper LF coil antenna tuned to 125 kHz, the EM4305 die with 512-bit EEPROM and a 32-bit password-lock cell, the 304 / 316 stainless split ring, and the potting that seals the cavity.

bullets: Housing options: ABS in 10+ pantone colours, platinum-cured silicone rated IP68 (IEC 60529, Shore A 60), or a seamless epoxy drop for outdoor duty.
LF coil antenna: a many-turn copper coil tuned to 125 kHz does all the energy harvesting — there is no battery.
EM4305 die: 512-bit EEPROM with a 32-bit password-lock cell, bonded to the coil and sealed in potting.
Split ring: 304 or 316 stainless steel — the part that actually fails first on a busy keyring.

faq.question: Can {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} keyfobs emulate HID proximity cards?
faq.answer: Yes. {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} supports configurable data encoding and modulation that can emulate HID 26-bit (H10301) and other HID Prox formats. You program the facility code and card number into the {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} chip using a 125 kHz RFID writer, and the keyfob responds to HID ProxPoint readers as if it were a genuine HID card. Note: this emulation works for basic HID Prox protocols; HID iCLASS (13.56 MHz) requires a different chip.

faq.question: How many times can the {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} be reprogrammed?
faq.answer: The {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} EEPROM is rated for 100,000 write cycles. In a typical access control deployment where a keyfob is reprogrammed once per tenant turnover (1-2 times per year), the chip will outlast the physical keyfob housing by orders of magnitude. There is no practical rewrite limit for access control applications.

faq.question: What is the MOQ and lead time?
faq.answer: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} keyfobs in standard ABS housing: MOQ 100, lead time 3-5 business days from stock. Custom-colored or silicone housing: MOQ 500, lead time 10-12 business days. Pre-programmed with your facility code or protocol emulation: add 1-2 business days to standard lead time. Volume pricing available at 500, 1,000 and 5,000+ quantities.

faq.question: Should I be worried about {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} keyfob cloning?
faq.answer: It depends on the threat model. 125 kHz LF chips — {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name}, {chip:atmel-t5577:name} and HID Prox II — have no cryptographic authentication at the air interface. A consumer Proxmark 3 or Flipper Zero can read the ID in seconds. This is a property of LF Prox as a whole, not {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} specifically. For low-stakes applications (apartment common areas, storage unit access, gym lockers, tenant turnover reuse) this is the accepted trade-off for low cost and universal legacy compatibility. For enterprise access, hotel rooms, controlled substances or transit fare, migrate the deployment to HF 13.56 MHz with AES-128 (MIFARE Plus SE, DESFire EV3) or HID iCLASS SE / Seos.

faq.question: Can {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} coexist with my HF 13.56 MHz reader on a dual-frequency migration?
faq.answer: Yes. A dual-frequency keyfob carries both an {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} (or {chip:atmel-t5577:name}) LF chip and a HF chip (typically MIFARE DESFire EV3 or an NTAG) in the same housing. The LF chip is read by existing 125 kHz proximity readers; the HF chip is read by new 13.56 MHz readers. Users keep the same fob through a multi-year reader-migration programme. See the [dual-frequency keyfob](/products/rfid-keyfobs/dual-frequency-key-fob/) SKU for specification details.

faq.question: Can EM4305 keyfobs be pre-programmed and branded with our logo and colours?
faq.answer: Yes. EM4305 keyfobs ship in ABS with 10+ pantone colour options and can be pad-printed or laser-marked with a logo and a sequential human-readable serial. Pre-programming is available: EM4100 emulation with sequential IDs, or HID Prox with your facility code and card-number range, delivered in labelled bags sorted by tenant, floor or building. Standard ABS is MOQ 100 (lead time 3-5 business days); custom-colour or silicone housing is MOQ 500 (10-12 business days); pre-programming adds 1-2 business days.
